title: Regression to Mean
hook: After the worst week, almost any next week can look like a miracle cure.
coreIdea: Regression to the mean means extreme results often move back toward typical levels, and that natural rebound can be mistaken for the effect of the last intervention.
counterintuition: A rebound after any intervention is not automatic proof that the intervention worked. First ask whether the starting result was unusually extreme and likely to soften anyway.
tryThisNow: Before crediting a fix, compare the before result with the usual range. Ask whether the next result simply moved back toward normal.
keyTakeaway: Do not give the last action credit for a rebound until you compare it with ordinary variation.

breakdown.fastRead:
A roast curve card sits beside the coffee supplier contract after one terrible shipment. Miriam threatens to switch suppliers. The next batch tastes better, and the warning looks powerful. It may be. It may also be the usual bounce from an unusually bad batch.

Regression to the mean hides inside rebounds. Very bad results often get less bad. Very good results often get less good. The movement can happen without the last scolding, bonus, policy, or ritual causing it.

Extreme is not the same as permanent.

The correction is to compare the result with the normal range before telling a causal story about the last action.
breakdown.deepRead:
The roast curve card in Miriam's cupping room shows one batch far below the supplier's usual score. It was not just weak; it was the worst shipment in months. Miriam complained, the next batch improved, and the team wants to say the complaint worked. She writes regression to mean on the card and pulls the last twelve shipment scores.

The complaint might have helped. Regression to the mean does not say interventions never matter. It says that extreme outcomes are special. They often contain a mix of real signal and temporary noise: weather, staffing, measurement, timing, luck. When the next result moves closer to normal, the mind gives the nearest visible action too much credit.

A rebound needs a comparison, not a story.

Miriam checks whether batches usually recover after extreme lows even without a formal complaint. If they do, the supplier warning gets less credit. If the recovery is larger than the normal bounce and the supplier changed a process, the warning may deserve some credit. The point is not to deny cause. The point is to stop confusing statistical drift with proof.

A neonatal checklist review shows the same trap with higher stakes. Oskar is holding a queue slip after a night with an unusually high number of transfer delays. The unit supervisor criticized the night staff, and the next shift improved. Oskar marks extreme outcome on the slip and asks for delay rates after every unusually bad night before praising the reprimand.

The next result often gets a head start toward normal.
breakdown.fullRead:
Cold air leaks under the shelter office door while Anya reads a timeline strip from the winter overflow desk. One night had a surge of missed beds. The next night improved after the director scolded the intake team. Several people now believe punishment works. Anya writes flight instructors on the strip before changing the staffing rule.

The flight-instructor example is famous because it feels so convincing. In teaching, instructors may see a trainee perform unusually well after praise and then worse next time, or unusually badly after criticism and then better next time. It is tempting to conclude that praise harms and punishment helps. Daniel Kahneman used this pattern to show how regression to the mean can impersonate a teaching effect.

What would have happened after an extreme result if no one had intervened?

That question protects the review. Anya does not excuse the missed beds. She compares the bad night with weather, intake volume, volunteer shortages, and past extreme nights. She asks whether the next-night rebound was beyond the usual bounce after a surge. If it was ordinary, the scolding gets no special credit. If a new intake step explains a larger improvement, that step can stay.

You can see the same mistake on a training field. You are watching Tom run a goalkeeper academy drill after one player has a terrible session. The coach scolds him, and the next session looks better. Tom marks praise risk on a glove warranty tag and must decide whether the scolding helped or whether a very bad session was likely to move closer to the player's usual level.

This is the useful middle: feedback can work, and regression can fool you.

Good feedback changes behavior through a mechanism: clearer cues, better timing, different practice, more sleep, safer equipment. Regression only changes the number's distance from normal. If you cannot separate those two, you will reward harshness after bad outliers and distrust praise after good outliers.

A flood insurance desk faces the same temptation after a claim spike. Petra sees one month of claims far above the usual band, then watches claims fall after premiums rise. The premium change may matter, but a spike that extreme was likely to cool. Petra has to compare the drop with earlier spikes before deciding whether customers changed behavior or the month simply moved back toward the mean.

So build a habit for postmortems. Before crediting the last action, ask whether the starting point was extreme. Then ask how similar extreme cases moved before. Only after that should you assign credit to praise, punishment, policy, coaching, or process change. The rebound may be real progress. It just has to beat the bounce.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Regression to the mean can make weak interventions look strong and useful feedback look weak. Readers need to compare rebounds with ordinary variation before assigning cause.

reviewCards.front: A terrible result improves after an intervention. What should you ask first?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the terrible result was extreme and likely to move back toward normal anyway.

reviewCards.front: Does regression to the mean prove feedback is useless?
reviewCards.back: No. It means you need a comparison before crediting feedback for a rebound.

reviewCards.front: Why can punishment look effective after bad performance?
reviewCards.back: Bad performance is often extreme. The next result may improve naturally, making punishment look causal.

reviewCards.front: Why can praise look harmful after great performance?
reviewCards.back: Great performance is often extreme. The next result may fall toward average even if praise did nothing wrong.
Look at similar extreme cases before and ask how they moved with and without the intervention.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to compare rebounds after extreme outcomes with ordinary variation before assigning credit to praise, punishment, policy, or coaching.

ifThenPlans.plan: If performance rebounds after a reprimand, then I will compare it with past rebounds after similarly bad results before crediting the reprimand.
If a great session is followed by an ordinary one, then I will check the athlete's normal range before blaming praise.
If a policy follows an extreme spike, then I will compare the next result with past spikes before declaring success.
If a fix seems to work after my worst week, then I will ask whether the week was an outlier and what usually happens next.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, find one rebound you were about to explain. Check whether the starting point was unusually high or low before naming the cause.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review one metric after an extreme result and compare the next result with at least three past rebounds.
